content_metadata.description: This video documentary explores the AST/RO telescope at the South Pole, its unique setting, and its research delving into the mysteries at the center of the Milky Way Galaxy.

qAndA.answer: Negative 49 degrees Celsius, or negative 118 degrees Fahrenheit.
qAndA.question: What is the average yearly temperature at the South Pole?

qAndA.answer: Because at the South Pole's high elevation of almost three thousand meters above sea level, it presents a unique window for radio astronomy. The dry, cold air is almost free of water vapor, allowing for free passage of the submillimeter signals emanating from the galactic center and cosmic microwave background.
qAndA.question: Why do astronomers brave the extreme conditions of the South Pole to do research?
What type of orbit is the gas that the researchers are observing in?
What causes noise in the telescopes' observations?

qAndA.answer: The South Pole has very low levels of atmospheric noise compared to other locations on Earth. The extremely cold and dry conditions minimize the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, which allows radio waves to pass through more easily.
qAndA.question: Why is the South Pole an ideal place to make these types of observations?

climax.description: Tony Stark explains that the gas builds up into a ring, which becomes thicker and thicker. Eventually a gravitational instability sets in, the ring coagulates into a giant cloud, then spirals into the galactic center by dynamical friction. This fuels the black hole at the center of the galaxy and makes the Milky Way an active galaxy.

youtube_description: AST/RO was a submillimeter-wave telescope at the South Pole, in operation from 1995 until 2005.  It was used for heterodyne spectroscopy of atoms and molecules in the Milky Way, and served as a prototype for the South Pole 10 meter telescope.  Featured scientist is Dr. Antony A. Stark of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.  Video by Dr. Gregory A. Wright.
